# Design picker — a Shiny app for generating statistical experimental designs.
#
# Pick a design in the sidebar, set its options, and download the run table.
#
# Run with shiny::runApp() from this directory. Everything in R/ is sourced
# automatically before this file, so there is nothing to source by hand:
#
#   R/design.R            the design object and shared helpers
#   R/{name}-design.R     the generator, pure R
#   R/{name}-module.R     its Shiny module
#   R/registry.R          the registry and the sidebar picker
#   R/ui.R, R/server.R    the page and how it updates

# What the app itself needs. Each design names its own packages through
# {design}_get_packages(), so adding a design that wraps a new package does not
# mean editing a list here.

require(shiny)
require(bslib)
require(reactable)
require(tibble)

shiny::shinyApp(app_ui(), app_server)

name: R/server.R
content:
# How the pieces update each other.
#
#   picker ---> selected() ---+--> output$options     (the design's own inputs)
#                             |
#                             v
#   design inputs --> current() --+--> output$summary
#   randomize ------------------^ +--> output$table
#                                 +--> output$download

app_server <- function(input, output, session) {
  registry <- design_registry()
  selected <- picker_server("picker")

  # Every module's server is started once, here. Their reactives stay lazy, so
  # an unselected design never runs its generator; only the one read by
  # current() below does.
  designs <- lapply(names(registry), function(id) registry[[id]]$server(id))
  names(designs) <- names(registry)

  output$options <- shiny::renderUI({
    shiny::req(selected())
    registry[[selected()]]$ui(selected())
  })

  current <- shiny::reactive({
    # req() is load-bearing, not decoration: `list[[NULL]]` is an error rather
    # than NULL, and selected() is briefly NULL while one family is cleared
    # and another set.
    shiny::req(selected())
    with_run_order(designs[[selected()]](), isTRUE(input$randomize))
  })

  output$summary <- shiny::renderUI({
    design <- current()
    shiny::tagList(
      shiny::p(shiny::strong(design$title)),
      lapply(design$notes, function(note) {
        shiny::p(class = "text-muted small", note)
      })
    )
  })

  output$table <- reactable::renderReactable({
    table <- display_table(current())
    factors <- setdiff(names(table), ORDER_COLUMNS)
    reactable::reactable(
      table,
      # Factor columns right-justified so digits line up on the units place;
      # the order columns keep the centred default so they still read as the
      # row labels they are.
      columns = stats::setNames(
        lapply(factors, function(...) reactable::colDef(align = "right")),
        factors
      ),
      # reactable paginates at 10 rows by default, which would cut a 16-run
      # design in half. Scroll inside a fixed height instead.
      pagination = FALSE,
      height = 480,
      compact = TRUE,
      striped = TRUE,
      defaultColDef = reactable::colDef(align = "center", minWidth = 80)
    )
  })

  # The CSV carries the numeric table, not the "+1" text the page shows.
  output$download <- shiny::downloadHandler(
    filename = function() paste0(selected(), ".csv"),
    content = function(file) {
      utils::write.csv(current()$table, file, row.names = FALSE)
    }
  )
}

# The design object every generator returns, and the helpers shared across
# designs. Nothing here depends on Shiny.

# The two order columns the app adds to the front of every design table.
ORDER_COLUMNS <- c("Standard order", "Run order")

# A design: the run table in standard order, a one-line title, and any notes to
# show beneath it, such as the defining relation.
#
# There was a `coded` flag here, but its only job was choosing between signed
# text and rounding in the display, and the table is no longer reformatted at
# all. Add it back if something actually needs to distinguish coded levels from
# real quantities.
new_design <- function(table, title, notes = character()) {
  # Coerced here so no generator has to remember. as_tibble() also drops row
  # names, which rbind() and friends otherwise leave behind. It does *not*
  # strip other attributes, so a generator wrapping a package still has to
  # hand over a clean table rather than the package's own object.
  structure(
    list(table = tibble::as_tibble(table), title = title, notes = notes),
    class = "doe_design"
  )
}

print.doe_design <- function(x, ...) {
  cat(x$title, "\n", sep = "")
  for (note in x$notes) {
    cat("  ", note, "\n", sep = "")
  }
  # Every run, rather than the tibble default of ten: a design is meant to be
  # read whole, and these are bounded by each design's own run ceiling.
  print(x$table, n = Inf)
  invisible(x)
}

# Stop with a message written for the person using the app, not for a
# developer: the module shows it in place of the table.
stop_unless <- function(condition, message) {
  if (!isTRUE(condition)) {
    stop(message, call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# A readable list of what is on offer, shortened when there is a lot of it.
format_choices <- function(x, max_shown = 12) {
  shown <- paste(utils::head(x, max_shown), collapse = ", ")
  if (length(x) > max_shown) {
    sprintf("%s, ... (%d in all)", shown, length(x))
  } else {
    shown
  }
}

# Report a value the underlying package cannot supply, and say what it can.
#
# Catalogued designs have irregular gaps rather than clean ranges — FrF2 has a
# 2048-run design for 34 factors but no 1024-run one, and around half of its
# factor counts have a hole like that. "Choose from this list" is the only
# honest message in that situation, and every package-backed design will need
# to give it, so this lives here rather than with any one design.
#
#   value     what was asked for
#   available what the package offers, possibly nothing
#   quantity  what is being chosen, such as "run count"
#   context   what it is being chosen for, such as "6 factors"
stop_unavailable <- function(value, available, quantity, context = NULL) {
  where <- if (is.null(context)) "" else paste0(" for ", context)
  if (length(available) == 0) {
    stop(sprintf("No %s is available%s.", quantity, where), call. = FALSE)
  }
  stop(
    sprintf(
      "%s is not an available %s%s. Choose one of: %s.",
      value,
      quantity,
      where,
      format_choices(available)
    ),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

# The same idea where the valid values really are a contiguous range, so
# listing them would be noise.
stop_out_of_range <- function(value, range, quantity) {
  stop(
    sprintf(
      "%s must be between %s and %s. Got %s.",
      quantity,
      range[1],
      range[2],
      value
    ),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

# Numbered labels: x1, x2, ... zero-padded once there are ten or more, so that
# x01 ... x10 stay in factor order. Used by factor_labels() below once the
# letters run out.
names0 <- function(num, prefix = "x") {
  ind <- format(seq_len(num))
  ind <- gsub(" ", "0", ind)
  paste0(prefix, ind)
}

# Default factor names: single letters while they last, then names0().
#
# Used both for default column names and for the alias notation — generators
# like "E = ABC" and defining relations like "I = ABCE". Those read well while
# the labels are one character each. Past 26 factors they cannot: the words
# concatenate, so "x001x002x003" is ambiguous. Nothing avoids that, since the
# letters have genuinely run out, and FrF2 has no longer letter vector of its
# own to borrow.
#
# What this is *not* used for is a user's own factor names. Those reach the
# columns only; the alias notation stays canonical, so renaming a factor to
# "Temp" never turns the defining relation into prose.
default_factor_names <- function(num_factors) {
  if (num_factors <= length(LETTERS)) {
    LETTERS[seq_len(num_factors)]
  } else {
    names0(num_factors)
  }
}

# Merge the user's comma-separated factor names over the defaults, giving
# exactly num_factors of them. Anything left out falls back to
# default_factor_names(); extra names are dropped; duplicates are made unique
# so two columns cannot share a header.
#
# The result feeds {design}_create(), which hands it to the underlying package.
# It must not be applied to a finished design instead: FrF2 needs the names at
# construction for its alias legend to read "A=Temp" rather than "A=A", and
# renaming afterwards would leave the notes describing factors by the wrong
# label.
rename_factors <- function(text, num_factors) {
  # Split on newlines as well as commas: the input is a text area, so one
  # name per line is a natural thing to type.
  given <- trimws(strsplit(text %||% "", "[,\n]")[[1]])
  given <- given[nzchar(given)]
  names <- default_factor_names(num_factors)
  supplied <- seq_len(min(length(given), num_factors))
  names[supplied] <- given[supplied]
  make.unique(names, sep = "_")
}

# Add the order columns. Generators are deterministic and return rows in
# standard order; randomizing permutes the order the runs are performed in and
# never the rows themselves, which is what keeps generator output snapshottable.
with_run_order <- function(design, randomize) {
  num_runs <- nrow(design$table)
  # add_column() rather than cbind(), which dispatches to the base method and
  # would hand back a plain data frame.
  design$table <- tibble::add_column(
    design$table,
    `Standard order` = seq_len(num_runs),
    `Run order` = if (randomize) sample(num_runs) else seq_len(num_runs),
    .before = 1
  )
  design
}

# The center-point clause of a design title, or "" when there are none.
center_point_text <- function(num_center, num_runs) {
  if (num_center < 1) {
    return("")
  }
  sprintf(
    " + %d center point%s (%d total)",
    num_center,
    if (num_center == 1) "" else "s",
    num_runs
  )
}

# Significant figures shown in the table.
DISPLAY_DIGITS <- 3L

# The table as the app displays it. Values are rounded for display and stay
# numeric — nothing is turned into text — and the CSV download writes the
# untouched table, so the file keeps full precision.
#
# signif() rather than reactable's colFormat(digits = ), which counts decimal
# places and would render a coded -1 as -1.000.
display_table <- function(design, digits = DISPLAY_DIGITS) {
  table <- design$table
  for (column in setdiff(names(table), ORDER_COLUMNS)) {
    if (is.numeric(table[[column]])) {
      table[[column]] <- signif(table[[column]], digits)
    }
  }
  table
}

name: R/factorial-design.R
content:
# Two-level factorial designs, full and fractional, from FrF2's catalog.
# Pure computation: no Shiny here, so every function below is testable on its
# own.
#
# This file implements the design contract described in the README:
#
#   factorial_get_packages()            packages this design needs
#   factorial_get_limits()              integer range of each count option
#   factorial_get_num_runs_choices()    valid run counts, given the factors
#   factorial_get_blocks_choices()      valid block counts, given the runs
#   factorial_get_types()               the variants to choose between
#   factorial_create()                  builds the doe_design
#   factorial_get_notes()               what the package says about the result
#
# Each states the shape it returns above it. The one worth reading twice is the
# *_choices() pair: the vector holds the values, and its names are the labels.
# Getting that backwards produces a dropdown that looks right and submits
# nonsense, because Shiny takes names as labels and values as values.

# Returns: an unnamed character vector of package names.
#
# Per design rather than one global list, because each design wraps a different
# package and the app should be able to name the one actually missing.
factorial_get_packages <- function() {
  c("DoE.base", "FrF2")
}

# The largest design this app offers. A practical limit of ours, not one of
# FrF2 — the installed catalog reaches 4096 runs and 160 factors, well past
# what anyone runs and past what the browser renders comfortably. It is
# declared here rather than in shared code because it belongs to this design;
# another design will have its own ceiling from its own package.
FACTORIAL_MAX_RUNS <- 256L

# Everything else about what this design supports is read off the installed
# catalog, so the app follows whichever FrF2 version is present rather than a
# second copy of its contents written out here. Computed once, when Shiny
# sources this file.
factorial_support <- local({
  num_factors <- vapply(FrF2::catlg, function(e) e$nfac, numeric(1))
  num_runs <- vapply(FrF2::catlg, function(e) e$nruns, numeric(1))
  keep <- num_runs <= FACTORIAL_MAX_RUNS
  lapply(split(num_runs[keep], num_factors[keep]), function(x) sort(unique(x)))
})

# The factor counts with at least one available design, as c(min, max).
factorial_factor_range <- local({
  catalogued <- as.integer(names(factorial_support))
  # Small factor counts have no catalogued fraction but do have a full
  # factorial. Two is where a factorial starts being one at all, which is
  # definitional rather than a limit of the package or a choice of ours.
  full_only <- Filter(
    function(num_factors) 2^num_factors <= FACTORIAL_MAX_RUNS,
    seq(2, max(catalogued))
  )
  range(c(catalogued, unlist(full_only)))
})

# Returns: a named list of integer vectors of length 2, each c(min, max)
# inclusive. Names are option names, so this design gives
# list(num_factors = c(2L, 127L)).
#
# A named list rather than a single range because not every design has one
# axis: a crossed array has separate control and noise factor counts, and a
# mixture design counts components rather than factors.
factorial_get_limits <- function() {
  list(num_factors = factorial_factor_range)
}

# Returns: a numeric vector of run counts, ascending, named by the label to
# show. Values are what gets passed back as num_runs; names are display only:
#
#   8 runs (2^(6-3) fraction)   16 runs (2^(6-2) fraction)
#                           8                           16
#
# Empty when this design supports no run count at that many factors. Feeds
# updateSelectInput(choices = ) directly.
#
# The run counts are the catalogued fractions plus the full factorial, when it
# is no larger than the biggest design the catalog holds.
#
# These are read off the catalog rather than computed as a span of powers of
# two. The catalog is irregular: 34 factors has a 2048-run design but no
# 1024-run one, and asking FrF2 for a size it lacks errors rather than
# returning nothing. Around half of its factor counts have a hole like that.
#
# All of those holes happen to sit above the current 256-run ceiling, so the
# arithmetic version would get away with it today. Reading the catalog means
# the app stays right if the ceiling is raised or a future FrF2 ships a
# different catalog, instead of depending on that coincidence.
factorial_get_num_runs_choices <- function(num_factors) {
  fractions <- factorial_support[[as.character(num_factors)]] %||% numeric(0)
  full <- if (2^num_factors <= FACTORIAL_MAX_RUNS) 2^num_factors else numeric(0)
  num_runs <- sort(unique(c(fractions, full)))
  labels <- ifelse(
    num_runs == 2^num_factors,
    sprintf("%d runs (full factorial)", num_runs),
    sprintf(
      "%d runs (2^(%d-%d) fraction)",
      num_runs,
      num_factors,
      num_factors - log2(num_runs)
    )
  )
  stats::setNames(num_runs, labels)
}

# The catalog designs of this size, best first: highest resolution, then the
# fewest words of that shortest length. A full factorial is not in the catalog,
# so this is empty for one.
factorial_catalog_entries <- function(num_factors, num_runs) {
  entries <- Filter(
    function(e) e$nfac == num_factors && e$nruns == num_runs,
    FrF2::catlg
  )
  if (length(entries) == 0) {
    return(entries)
  }
  resolution <- vapply(entries, function(e) e$res, numeric(1))
  shortest <- vapply(entries, function(e) e$WLP[e$res], numeric(1))
  utils::head(entries[order(-resolution, shortest)], 6)
}

# The label shown for one catalog design in the "Choose a design" radio.
# Generators come from DoE.base, already written as "E=ABC", rather than being
# decoded from the catalog's Yates column codes here.
factorial_type_label <- function(name, entry, max_generators = 6) {
  # select.catlg is passed explicitly: generators() defaults it to a bare
  # `catlg`, which is only on the search path if FrF2 has been attached, and
  # this app only ever uses FrF2:: qualified calls.
  generators <- DoE.base::generators(name, select.catlg = FrF2::catlg)[[1]]
  # A large design can have fifty-odd generators, which makes an unreadable
  # radio label. The resolution and word count are what tell the choices apart.
  shown <- paste(utils::head(generators, max_generators), collapse = ", ")
  if (length(generators) > max_generators) {
    shown <- sprintf("%s, ... (%d generators)", shown, length(generators))
  }
  shortest <- entry$WLP[entry$res]
  sprintf(
    "Resolution %s: %s (%d word%s of length %d)",
    as.character(utils::as.roman(entry$res)),
    shown,
    shortest,
    if (shortest == 1) "" else "s",
    entry$res
  )
}

# Returns: a character vector of catalog ids, best first, named by the label to
# show. Same values-and-names convention as the *_choices() helpers:
#
#   Resolution IV: E=ABC, F=ABD (3 words of length 4)
#                                            "6-2.1"
#
# Zero-length when there is nothing to choose — a full factorial has no catalog
# entry, and most other designs have no type at all — so callers must handle an
# empty result rather than assuming at least one.
factorial_get_types <- function(num_factors, num_runs) {
  entries <- factorial_catalog_entries(num_factors, num_runs)
  if (length(entries) == 0) {
    return(stats::setNames(character(0), character(0)))
  }
  stats::setNames(
    names(entries),
    vapply(
      names(entries),
      function(id) factorial_type_label(id, entries[[id]]),
      character(1)
    )
  )
}

# Returns: an unnamed character vector, one note per line to show under the
# title, or character(0) when there is nothing to say. Takes the object the
# package returned, not a doe_design.
#
# The alias structure FrF2 attaches to every design it builds, under
# attr(design, "design.info")$aliased. Reported, not derived.
#
# This used to be computed here, by multiplying every combination of the
# design's generators to get the defining relation. That is 2^p - 1 words for
# p generators: fine for the two a small design has, hopeless for the 24 in a
# 30-factor design (16.7 million) or the 53 in a 60-factor one (9e15). FrF2
# instead reports alias classes of two-factor interactions, which is bounded
# by the run count — 0.11s for that 60-factor design — and is what an
# experimenter wants to know anyway.
factorial_get_notes <- function(design) {
  aliased <- attr(design, "design.info")$aliased
  # A full factorial has no catalog entry and nothing aliased.
  if (is.null(aliased)) {
    return(character())
  }
  notes <- character()

  # The legend maps FrF2's own letters onto the factor names in use. It is
  # identity until a factor has been renamed, and noise until then.
  letters_used <- sub("=.*$", "", aliased$legend)
  names_used <- sub("^[^=]*=", "", aliased$legend)
  renamed <- aliased$legend[letters_used != names_used]
  if (length(renamed) > 0) {
    notes <- c(notes, paste0("Factors: ", format_choices(renamed)))
  }

  if (length(aliased$main) > 0) {
    notes <- c(
      notes,
      paste0("Main effects aliased: ", format_choices(aliased$main))
    )
  }
  if (length(aliased$fi2) > 0) {
    notes <- c(
      notes,
      paste0("Two-factor interactions aliased: ", format_choices(aliased$fi2))
    )
  }
  notes
}

# Returns: a numeric vector of block counts, ascending, unnamed — the number
# is its own label, so there is nothing to add. Names are optional across the
# *_choices() helpers; supply them only when the value alone does not read
# well, as the run counts do.
#
# Block counts are those FrF2 will consider, by its own two rules: a power of
# two, and no more blocks than half the run size.
#
# Whether a *particular* count works also depends on the design — FrF2 refuses
# a blocking that would confound a two-factor interaction with blocks, so 4
# blocks is fine for some 16-run designs and not for 6-2.1. That cannot be
# known without building the design, and probing every candidate takes 16s for
# a 256-run design, which is far too slow for a dropdown. So offer what is
# structurally valid and let FrF2's own message cover the rest; the module
# shows it in place of the table.
factorial_get_blocks_choices <- function(num_runs) {
  2^(0:floor(log2(num_runs / 2)))
}

# Returns: a doe_design — see new_design(). The table holds one row per run in
# standard order, with FrF2's block column first when there is one; the order
# columns are added later, by the app.
#
# A two-level factorial design.
#
#   num_factors  within factorial_get_limits()$num_factors
#   num_runs     one of factorial_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors)
#   type         which catalog design to use when several are equivalent, as an
#                id from factorial_get_types(). NULL takes the best one, and is
#                the only valid value for a full factorial, which has no types.
#   center       center points per block
#   blocks       one of factorial_get_blocks_choices(num_runs)
#   replications times each run is carried out
#   factor_names column names, one per factor
#
# center, blocks and replications default to FrF2's own defaults.
factorial_create <- function(
  num_factors,
  num_runs,
  type = NULL,
  center = 0,
  blocks = 1,
  replications = 1,
  factor_names = default_factor_names(num_factors)
) {
  # Checked before the range comparison below, which would otherwise be NA and
  # fail with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" rather than a message.
  stop_unless(
    length(num_factors) == 1 &&
      !is.na(num_factors) &&
      num_factors == round(num_factors),
    "Number of factors must be a whole number."
  )
  if (
    num_factors < factorial_factor_range[1] ||
      num_factors > factorial_factor_range[2]
  ) {
    stop_out_of_range(num_factors, factorial_factor_range, "Number of factors")
  }
  available <- factorial_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors)
  if (!num_runs %in% available) {
    stop_unavailable(
      num_runs,
      available,
      "run count",
      sprintf("%d factors", num_factors)
    )
  }
  stop_unless(center >= 0, "Center points cannot be negative.")
  stop_unless(
    replications >= 1 && replications == round(replications),
    "Replications must be a whole number of at least 1."
  )
  available_blocks <- factorial_get_blocks_choices(num_runs)
  if (!blocks %in% available_blocks) {
    stop_unavailable(
      blocks,
      available_blocks,
      "block count",
      sprintf("%d runs", num_runs)
    )
  }
  # as.numeric deliberately. FrF2's `blocks` is overloaded: a number means how
  # many blocks, but a vector of Yates column numbers is also accepted. An
  # integer 1L takes the latter branch and fails with "'names' attribute [2]
  # must be the same length as the vector [0]" instead of meaning "unblocked".
  # A double 1 means what we want.
  blocks <- as.numeric(blocks)
  stop_unless(
    length(factor_names) == num_factors,
    sprintf("Give %d factor names, not %d.", num_factors, length(factor_names))
  )
  # FrF2 adds its block column under this name, so a factor cannot take it.
  stop_unless(
    blocks == 1 || !"Blocks" %in% factor_names,
    "\"Blocks\" is reserved for the block column; rename that factor."
  )

  # factor.names is passed to FrF2 rather than applied to the table
  # afterwards, so that the alias structure it attaches is expressed in the
  # names actually in use — its legend reads "A=Temp" instead of "A=A".
  # ncenter is FrF2's own, rather than appending zero rows here. With
  # randomize = FALSE it puts them at the end, which is what we were doing by
  # hand; it also records them in design.info, and its center.distribute
  # argument can spread them through the run order if that is ever wanted.
  types <- factorial_get_types(num_factors, num_runs)
  if (length(types) == 0) {
    # A full factorial, which the catalog does not hold and which has no
    # variants to choose between.
    design <- suppressMessages(FrF2::FrF2(
      nruns = num_runs,
      nfactors = num_factors,
      randomize = FALSE,
      factor.names = factor_names,
      ncenter = center,
      blocks = blocks,
      replications = replications
    ))
    description <- sprintf("2^%d full factorial", num_factors)
  } else {
    # Identified by catalog id rather than by position, so a type left over
    # from a different size is rejected by name instead of silently selecting
    # whatever now sits at that index.
    if (is.null(type)) {
      type <- unname(types[1])
    }
    if (!type %in% types) {
      stop_unavailable(
        type,
        types,
        "design",
        sprintf("%d factors in %d runs", num_factors, num_runs)
      )
    }
    entry <- FrF2::catlg[[type]]
    design <- suppressMessages(FrF2::FrF2(
      design = type,
      randomize = FALSE,
      factor.names = factor_names,
      ncenter = center,
      blocks = blocks,
      replications = replications
    ))
    description <- sprintf(
      "2^(%d-%d) fractional factorial, resolution %s",
      num_factors,
      num_factors - log2(num_runs),
      as.character(utils::as.roman(entry$res))
    )
  }

  # The design itself rather than desnum(): it carries FrF2's factor names and
  # a readable Blocks column, where desnum() contrast-codes that column into
  # Blocks1.
  #
  # The block column keeps its labels rather than being made numeric. With
  # replications FrF2 labels blocks "1.1", "2.1" — block and replicate, not a
  # decimal — so coercing would turn "1.1" into 1.1 and quietly invent a
  # number. It is found by elimination because design.info$block.name is NULL
  # when replications alone produced the column.
  # Rebuilt as a plain data frame rather than modified in place: FrF2 carries
  # design.info, desnum and run.order as attributes on the design, and those
  # should not ride along on the table we hand out.
  raw <- as.data.frame(design)
  factor_columns <- intersect(names(raw), factor_names)
  columns <- lapply(names(raw), function(column) {
    values <- raw[[column]]
    if (!column %in% factor_columns) {
      as.character(values)
    } else if (is.factor(values)) {
      as.numeric(as.character(values))
    } else {
      as.numeric(values)
    }
  })
  names(columns) <- names(raw)
  table <- tibble::as_tibble(columns)

  new_design(
    table,
    sprintf(
      "%s – %d factors, %d runs%s%s%s",
      description,
      num_factors,
      num_runs,
      if (blocks > 1) sprintf(", %d blocks", blocks) else "",
      if (replications > 1) {
        sprintf(", %d replications", replications)
      } else {
        ""
      },
      # ncenter is per block, so this many in total.
      center_point_text(center * blocks, nrow(table))
    ),
    factorial_get_notes(design)
  )
}

name: R/factorial-module.R
content:
# The Shiny module wrapping factorial_create(). The server returns a reactive
# yielding a doe_design, which is the whole contract the app depends on.

# The factor count the panel opens on. Named, because the dependent dropdowns
# below are built from it and the two must not drift apart.
FACTORIAL_DEFAULT_FACTORS <- 6L

factorial_ui <- function(id, num_factors = FACTORIAL_DEFAULT_FACTORS) {
  ns <- shiny::NS(id)
  # Populated here rather than left empty for the server to fill. The
  # observers below only fire when num_factors *changes*, and returning to a
  # design rebuilds this UI with the same value, which Shiny's input dedup
  # suppresses -- so the dropdowns would come back empty and stay empty until
  # the factor count was nudged.
  num_runs_choices <- factorial_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors)
  blocks_choices <- factorial_get_blocks_choices(num_runs_choices[[1]])
  shiny::tagList(
    shiny::numericInput(
      ns("num_factors"),
      "Number of factors",
      value = num_factors,
      min = factorial_get_limits()$num_factors[1],
      max = factorial_get_limits()$num_factors[2]
    ),
    shiny::selectInput(
      ns("num_runs"),
      "Number of runs",
      choices = num_runs_choices
    ),
    shiny::selectInput(
      ns("center"),
      "Center points per block",
      choices = 0:5,
      selected = 0
    ),
    shiny::selectInput(ns("blocks"), "Blocks", choices = blocks_choices),
    shiny::numericInput(ns("replications"), "Replications", value = 1, min = 1),
    # A text area rather than a single line: the list runs to one name per
    # factor, and the comma-separated form gets long.
    shiny::textAreaInput(
      ns("factor_names"),
      "Factor names",
      rows = 3,
      resize = "vertical",
      placeholder = "Temp, Pressure, Time — blank for A, B, C"
    ),
    # Unlike the dropdown above, this input's existence is conditional, not
    # just its choices, so it stays a renderUI.
    shiny::uiOutput(ns("types"))
  )
}

# Is this a factor count we can build a design from? Guards every reactive
# below, because moduleServer() runs eagerly at startup and input$num_factors
# is NULL until the UI has been rendered and bound.
usable_factor_count <- function(num_factors) {
  limits <- factorial_get_limits()$num_factors
  isTRUE(
    length(num_factors) == 1 &&
      !is.na(num_factors) &&
      num_factors == round(num_factors) &&
      num_factors >= limits[1] &&
      num_factors <= limits[2]
  )
}

factorial_server <- function(id) {
  shiny::moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    shiny::observeEvent(input$num_factors, {
      shiny::req(usable_factor_count(input$num_factors))
      shiny::updateSelectInput(
        session,
        "num_runs",
        choices = factorial_get_num_runs_choices(input$num_factors)
      )
    })

    # The run count the user picked, once it is one that suits the current
    # factor count. Just after num_factors changes the old value is briefly
    # still there.
    num_runs <- shiny::reactive({
      shiny::req(usable_factor_count(input$num_factors), input$num_runs)
      value <- as.numeric(input$num_runs)
      shiny::req(value %in% factorial_get_num_runs_choices(input$num_factors))
      value
    })

    # How many blocks are possible depends on the run count.
    shiny::observeEvent(num_runs(), {
      shiny::updateSelectInput(
        session,
        "blocks",
        choices = factorial_get_blocks_choices(num_runs())
      )
    })

    types <- shiny::reactive({
      factorial_get_types(as.integer(input$num_factors), num_runs())
    })

    # With fewer than two variants there is nothing to choose, so the input is
    # not drawn at all.
    output$types <- shiny::renderUI({
      available <- types()
      if (length(available) < 2) {
        return(NULL)
      }
      shiny::radioButtons(
        session$ns("type"),
        "Choose a design",
        choiceNames = names(available),
        choiceValues = unname(available),
        width = "100%"
      )
    })

    shiny::reactive({
      shiny::validate(shiny::need(
        usable_factor_count(input$num_factors),
        sprintf(
          "Enter a whole number of factors from %d to %d.",
          factorial_factor_range[1],
          factorial_factor_range[2]
        )
      ))
      shiny::req(input$center, input$blocks, input$replications)
      # The block choices are repopulated when the run count changes, so the
      # old value can briefly outlive the run count it belonged to.
      blocks <- as.numeric(input$blocks)
      shiny::req(blocks %in% factorial_get_blocks_choices(num_runs()))
      num_factors <- as.integer(input$num_factors)

      design <- tryCatch(
        factorial_create(
          num_factors = num_factors,
          num_runs = num_runs(),
          # Removing the radio does not clear the input, so a type can outlive
          # the size it belonged to. Falling back to the best available one is
          # a UI concern; factorial_create() itself rejects an unknown id.
          type = if (isTRUE(input$type %in% types())) input$type else NULL,
          center = as.integer(input$center),
          blocks = blocks,
          replications = as.integer(input$replications),
          factor_names = rename_factors(input$factor_names, num_factors)
        ),
        error = function(e) e
      )
      if (inherits(design, "error")) {
        shiny::validate(shiny::need(FALSE, conditionMessage(design)))
      }
      design
    })
  })
}

name: R/registry.R
content:
# Where designs are registered, and the sidebar that picks between them.
#
# To add a design: write R/<name>-design.R and R/<name>-module.R, then add one
# entry below. Nothing else in the app needs to change.

DEFAULT_DESIGN <- "factorial"

# A function rather than a plain list, deliberately. Shiny sources R/ in
# alphabetical order, so a design file sorting after this one (R/rsm-module.R
# would) is not yet loaded when this file runs. Resolving the functions when
# the registry is called instead of when it is defined makes the order
# irrelevant.
# Order matters: families appear in the sidebar in the order they are first
# used here, and designs in the order they are listed within a family.
design_registry <- function() {
  list(
    lhs_random = list(
      label = "Latin hypercubes (Random)",
      family = "Space-Filling Designs",
      ui = spacefilling_rand_ui,
      server = spacefilling_rand_server,
      packages = spacefilling_rand_get_packages
    ),
    lhs_optimized = list(
      label = "Latin hypercubes (Optimized)",
      family = "Space-Filling Designs",
      ui = spacefilling_opt_ui,
      server = spacefilling_opt_server,
      packages = spacefilling_opt_get_packages
    ),
    uniform = list(
      label = "Uniform designs",
      family = "Space-Filling Designs",
      ui = spacefilling_unif_ui,
      server = spacefilling_unif_server,
      packages = spacefilling_unif_get_packages
    ),
    factorial = list(
      label = "Two-level factorial",
      family = "Screening designs",
      ui = factorial_ui,
      server = factorial_server,
      packages = factorial_get_packages
    ),
    taguchi = list(
      label = "Two-level Taguchi",
      family = "Screening designs",
      ui = taguchi_ui,
      server = taguchi_server,
      packages = taguchi_get_packages
    )
  )
}

# Design ids grouped by family, families in the order they first appear.
design_families <- function(registry = design_registry()) {
  families <- vapply(registry, function(d) d$family, character(1))
  split(names(registry), factor(families, levels = unique(families)))
}

# The picker is one accordion panel per family with a radio group inside each.
# Exactly one design is selected across the whole app, so choosing in one
# family clears every other.
picker_ui <- function(
  id,
  registry = design_registry(),
  selected = DEFAULT_DESIGN
) {
  ns <- shiny::NS(id)
  families <- design_families(registry)

  panels <- lapply(seq_along(families), function(i) {
    ids <- families[[i]]
    bslib::accordion_panel(
      title = names(families)[i],
      value = names(families)[i],
      # The design-picker class is what the stylesheet in R/ui.R hangs the
      # link styling on. The control stays a radio group; it just does not
      # look like one.
      shiny::tagAppendAttributes(
        class = "design-picker",
        shiny::radioButtons(
          ns(paste0("family_", i)),
          label = NULL,
          choiceNames = unname(vapply(
            ids,
            function(x) registry[[x]]$label,
            character(1)
          )),
          choiceValues = ids,
          # character(0) leaves the group unchecked. NULL would silently
          # select the first choice, which would mean several families
          # claiming a selection at once.
          selected = if (selected %in% ids) selected else character(0)
        )
      )
    )
  })

  open <- names(families)[
    vapply(families, function(ids) selected %in% ids, logical(1))
  ]

  # Returned bare, not wrapped in a tagList or div: bslib only renders an
  # accordion flush against the sidebar when it is an immediate child of it.
  do.call(
    bslib::accordion,
    c(list(id = ns("family"), multiple = FALSE, open = open), panels)
  )
}

# Returns a reactive holding the id of the selected design.
picker_server <- function(
  id,
  registry = design_registry(),
  default = DEFAULT_DESIGN
) {
  shiny::moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    families <- design_families(registry)
    inputs <- paste0("family_", seq_along(families))
    selected <- shiny::reactiveVal(default)

    # lapply(), not a for loop: R does not rebind a loop variable per
    # iteration, so a for loop here would leave every observer pointing at the
    # last family.
    lapply(seq_along(inputs), function(i) {
      shiny::observeEvent(
        input[[inputs[i]]],
        {
          selected(input[[inputs[i]]])
          for (other in inputs[-i]) {
            # This cannot feed back. Clearing a family that is already clear
            # sends an identical value, which Shiny's client drops before it
            # reaches the server; the one family that did hold a selection sends
            # NULL, which ignoreNULL stops before the handler body runs.
            shiny::updateRadioButtons(session, other, selected = character(0))
          }
        },
        ignoreNULL = TRUE
      )
    })

    selected
  })
}

name: R/taguchi-design.R
content:
# Two-level Taguchi orthogonal arrays, from DoE.base's catalog. Pure
# computation: no Shiny here, so every function below is testable on its own.
#
# This file implements the design contract described in the README:
#
#   taguchi_get_packages()            packages this design needs
#   taguchi_get_limits()              integer range of the factor count
#   taguchi_get_num_runs_choices()    valid run counts, given the factors
#   taguchi_create()                  builds the doe_design
#   taguchi_get_notes()               what the package says about the result
#
# There is no taguchi_get_types(): one array exists per run count, so there is
# nothing to choose between.

# Returns: an unnamed character vector of package names.
taguchi_get_packages <- function() {
  "DoE.base"
}

# The arrays this design offers, read off DoE.base's catalog: one row each, in
# ascending run order, with the catalog's own name, its run count and its
# number of columns.
#
# "Two-level Taguchi" is the saturated arrays L_N(2^(N-1)): every column is
# two-level, and there is one column for each degree of freedom the runs
# provide. The saturation test is what separates them from L256.2.19 and
# L2048.2.63, which also hold only two-level columns but are fractions of a
# much larger array. It is the definition of the family rather than a ceiling
# of ours, so none is declared; the largest array comes out at 140 runs.
#
# Computed once, when Shiny sources this file. The catalog has no gaps in its
# run counts today, but they are read rather than computed as a span so that
# the app follows whichever DoE.base version is installed.
taguchi_support <- local({
  catalog <- DoE.base::oacat
  level_columns <- grep("^n[0-9]+$", names(catalog), value = TRUE)
  other_levels <- setdiff(level_columns, "n2")
  saturated <- catalog$n2 > 0 &
    rowSums(catalog[other_levels]) == 0 &
    catalog$n2 == catalog$nruns - 1
  support <- data.frame(
    name = catalog$name[saturated],
    num_runs = as.integer(catalog$nruns[saturated]),
    num_columns = as.integer(catalog$n2[saturated]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  support[order(support$num_runs), ]
})

# Returns: a named list of integer vectors of length 2, each c(min, max)
# inclusive, so this design gives list(num_factors = c(2L, 139L)).
#
# Two is where an array starts being a design at all. The top is the widest
# array in the catalog.
taguchi_get_limits <- function() {
  list(num_factors = c(2L, max(taguchi_support$num_columns)))
}

# Returns: a numeric vector of run counts, ascending, named by the label to
# show. Values are what gets passed back as num_runs; names are display only:
#
#   8 runs (L8)   12 runs (L12)
#               8             12
#
# An array is offered when it has a column for every factor, so the smallest
# is first. Empty past the widest array. Feeds updateSelectInput(choices = )
# directly.
taguchi_get_num_runs_choices <- function(num_factors) {
  wide_enough <- taguchi_support[taguchi_support$num_columns >= num_factors, ]
  stats::setNames(
    as.numeric(wide_enough$num_runs),
    sprintf("%d runs (L%d)", wide_enough$num_runs, wide_enough$num_runs)
  )
}

# The one place oa.design() is called, so its quirks are explained once.
#
# The array is pinned by its catalog id. The alternative, handing oa.design()
# only nruns, nfactors and nlevels = 2, lets it choose an array by its own
# criteria, and it does not choose these ones: it returns a replicated full
# factorial for small factor counts and a mixed-level array such as L32.2.9 or
# L96.2.20.4.2 for others.
#
# oa.design() reads ID as an unevaluated name, and rejects a character string.
# A name it cannot find as an object it looks up in the catalog and builds from
# its lineage, which works for most arrays. The base arrays (L4.2.3, L12.2.11
# and every fourth one after) have no lineage, so for those the object is bound
# to its own name first. Without that they fail with "No lineage information
# found".
#
# replications stacks complete copies of the array, in standard order, with
# nothing added to mark which copy a row belongs to. repeat.only is left at its
# default, FALSE: a true replication, rather than the same run measured twice.
#
# columns is left at the package default, "order": the first num_factors
# columns, which oa.design() announces with a message that is not for the
# experimenter.
#
# factor.names is deliberately not passed. oa.design() runs the names through
# make.names(), so "Temp (C)" becomes "Temp..C." and "1st" becomes "X1st", which
# is not what the experimenter typed. taguchi_create() applies the names to the
# table instead. The usual objection to renaming afterwards, that the package's
# notes would describe the factors by the wrong label, does not arise: nothing
# in this design's notes mentions a factor by name.
taguchi_oa_design <- function(id, num_factors, replications = 1) {
  env <- new.env()
  base_array <- tryCatch(
    getExportedValue("DoE.base", id),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(base_array)) {
    assign(id, base_array, envir = env)
  }
  suppressMessages(eval(
    bquote(DoE.base::oa.design(
      ID = .(as.name(id)),
      nfactors = .(num_factors),
      replications = .(replications),
      randomize = FALSE
    )),
    envir = env
  ))
}

# Returns: an unnamed character vector, one note per line to show under the
# title. Takes the object the package returned, not a doe_design.
#
# All of it is read from design.info, which oa.design() attaches: the columns
# of the array that were used, and the residual degrees of freedom it works
# out. Reported, not derived. The levels line is ours to state, since the
# package hands back a factor labelled "1" and "2" and create() recodes it.
# The package labels the two levels "1" and "2". They are recoded to -1 and +1
# so this design reads on the same scale as the two-level factorial. Declared
# here, by label, rather than inferred from the values in a table.
TAGUCHI_CODED <- c("1" = -1, "2" = 1)

taguchi_get_notes <- function(design) {
  info <- attr(design, "design.info")
  array_columns <- taguchi_support$num_columns[
    taguchi_support$num_runs == info$nruns
  ]
  columns_used <- info$selected.columns
  c(
    if (length(columns_used) == array_columns) {
      sprintf("Uses all %d columns of the array.", array_columns)
    } else {
      sprintf(
        "Uses columns %s of the array's %d.",
        format_choices(columns_used),
        array_columns
      )
    },
    "Levels are coded -1 and +1.",
    sprintf(
      "Residual degrees of freedom%s: %d.",
      # oa.design() works this out from the array alone and does not count
      # replication, so with replicates the figure understates what the table
      # has. Said so rather than corrected here, since the package is the
      # source of truth for the number.
      if (info$replications > 1) ", not counting replication" else "",
      info$residual.df
    )
  )
}

# Returns: a doe_design — see new_design(). The table holds one row per run in
# standard order; the order columns are added later, by the app.
#
# A two-level Taguchi orthogonal array.
#
#   num_factors  within taguchi_get_limits()$num_factors
#   num_runs     one of taguchi_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors)
#   replications times each run is carried out; the array is stacked that many
#                times, so the table has num_runs * replications rows
#   factor_names column names, one per factor
taguchi_create <- function(
  num_factors,
  num_runs,
  replications = 1,
  factor_names = default_factor_names(num_factors)
) {
  limits <- taguchi_get_limits()$num_factors
  # Checked before the range comparison below, which would otherwise be NA and
  # fail with "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" rather than a message.
  stop_unless(
    length(num_factors) == 1 &&
      !is.na(num_factors) &&
      num_factors == round(num_factors),
    "Number of factors must be a whole number."
  )
  if (num_factors < limits[1] || num_factors > limits[2]) {
    stop_out_of_range(num_factors, limits, "Number of factors")
  }
  stop_unless(
    length(num_runs) == 1 && !is.na(num_runs),
    "Number of runs must be a single number."
  )
  available <- taguchi_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors)
  if (!num_runs %in% available) {
    stop_unavailable(
      num_runs,
      available,
      "run count",
      sprintf("%d factors", num_factors)
    )
  }
  stop_unless(
    length(replications) == 1 &&
      !is.na(replications) &&
      replications >= 1 &&
      replications == round(replications),
    "Replications must be a whole number of at least 1."
  )
  stop_unless(
    length(factor_names) == num_factors,
    sprintf("Give %d factor names, not %d.", num_factors, length(factor_names))
  )

  id <- taguchi_support$name[taguchi_support$num_runs == num_runs]
  design <- taguchi_oa_design(id, num_factors, as.numeric(replications))

  # Rebuilt column by column as plain numbers. oa.design() returns each factor
  # as an R factor with levels "1" and "2" and carries design.info on the
  # object; neither should ride along on the table we hand out. Recoded by
  # label through TAGUCHI_CODED, never by the factor's integer codes, which
  # would only agree with the label by coincidence.
  raw <- as.data.frame(design)
  columns <- lapply(raw, function(values) {
    coded <- unname(TAGUCHI_CODED[as.character(values)])
    stop_unless(
      !anyNA(coded),
      "DoE.base returned a level this design does not recognise."
    )
    coded
  })
  names(columns) <- factor_names
  table <- tibble::as_tibble(columns)

  new_design(
    table,
    sprintf(
      "L%d orthogonal array (2^%d) – %d factors, %d runs%s",
      num_runs,
      num_runs - 1,
      num_factors,
      num_runs,
      if (replications > 1) sprintf(", %d replications", replications) else ""
    ),
    taguchi_get_notes(design)
  )
}

# The Shiny module wrapping taguchi_create(). The server returns a reactive
# yielding a doe_design, which is the whole contract the app depends on.

# The factor count the panel opens on. Named, because the run dropdown below is
# built from it and the two must not drift apart. Seven is what the L8, the
# smallest array offered for it, is saturated by.
TAGUCHI_DEFAULT_FACTORS <- 7L

taguchi_ui <- function(id, num_factors = TAGUCHI_DEFAULT_FACTORS) {
  ns <- shiny::NS(id)
  # Populated here rather than left empty for the server to fill. The observer
  # below only fires when num_factors *changes*, and returning to a design
  # rebuilds this UI with the same value, which Shiny's input dedup suppresses
  # -- so the dropdown would come back empty and stay empty until the factor
  # count was nudged.
  shiny::tagList(
    shiny::numericInput(
      ns("num_factors"),
      "Number of factors",
      value = num_factors,
      min = taguchi_get_limits()$num_factors[1],
      max = taguchi_get_limits()$num_factors[2]
    ),
    shiny::selectInput(
      ns("num_runs"),
      "Number of runs",
      choices = taguchi_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors)
    ),
    shiny::numericInput(ns("replications"), "Replications", value = 1, min = 1),
    shiny::textAreaInput(
      ns("factor_names"),
      "Factor names",
      rows = 3,
      resize = "vertical",
      placeholder = "Temp, Pressure, Time — blank for A, B, C"
    )
  )
}

# Is this a factor count we can build a design from? Guards every reactive
# below, because moduleServer() runs eagerly at startup and input$num_factors
# is NULL until the UI has been rendered and bound.
taguchi_usable_factor_count <- function(num_factors) {
  limits <- taguchi_get_limits()$num_factors
  isTRUE(
    length(num_factors) == 1 &&
      !is.na(num_factors) &&
      num_factors == round(num_factors) &&
      num_factors >= limits[1] &&
      num_factors <= limits[2]
  )
}

taguchi_server <- function(id) {
  shiny::moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    shiny::observeEvent(input$num_factors, {
      shiny::req(taguchi_usable_factor_count(input$num_factors))
      shiny::updateSelectInput(
        session,
        "num_runs",
        choices = taguchi_get_num_runs_choices(input$num_factors)
      )
    })

    shiny::reactive({
      limits <- taguchi_get_limits()$num_factors
      shiny::validate(shiny::need(
        taguchi_usable_factor_count(input$num_factors),
        sprintf(
          "Enter a whole number of factors from %d to %d.",
          limits[1],
          limits[2]
        )
      ))
      shiny::req(input$num_runs, input$replications)
      num_factors <- as.integer(input$num_factors)
      # The run count the user picked, once it is one that suits the current
      # factor count. Just after num_factors changes the old value is briefly
      # still there.
      num_runs <- as.numeric(input$num_runs)
      shiny::req(num_runs %in% taguchi_get_num_runs_choices(num_factors))

      design <- tryCatch(
        taguchi_create(
          num_factors = num_factors,
          num_runs = num_runs,
          replications = as.integer(input$replications),
          factor_names = rename_factors(input$factor_names, num_factors)
        ),
        error = function(e) e
      )
      if (inherits(design, "error")) {
        shiny::validate(shiny::need(FALSE, conditionMessage(design)))
      }
      design
    })
  })
}

name: README.md
content:
# doe-ui

A Shiny interface to R's experimental design generators. Pick a design, set its options, and download the run table as CSV.

## Running

```r
shiny::runApp()
```

Needs R 4.4 or later and the packages `bslib`, `DiceDesign`, `DoE.base`, `FrF2`, `reactable`, `sfd`, `shiny` and `tibble`. The app checks for them on startup and names any that are missing — the per-design ones come from each `{design}_get_packages()`, so this list is derived rather than maintained by hand.

## Tests

```sh
Rscript tests/run.R
```

Output is checked with testthat snapshots, so review a diff before accepting it — a changed snapshot usually means a changed design, not a cosmetic difference.

## Layout

Shiny sources everything in `R/` automatically, so there is nothing to `source()` by hand.

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `app.R` | Package check, then `shinyApp()` |
| `R/design.R` | The `doe_design` object and the helpers every design shares |
| `R/factorial-design.R` | The two-level factorial generator — pure R, no Shiny |
| `R/factorial-module.R` | Its Shiny module |
| `R/taguchi-design.R` | The two-level Taguchi orthogonal arrays (DoE.base) — pure R, no Shiny |
| `R/taguchi-module.R` | Its Shiny module |
| `R/spacefilling-design.R` | The three space-filling generators: optimized hypercubes and uniform designs (sfd), and random hypercubes (DiceDesign) |
| `R/spacefilling-module.R` | Their Shiny modules |
| `R/registry.R` | The design registry and the sidebar picker |
| `R/ui.R`, `R/server.R` | The page, and how its pieces update each other |

## Adding a design

One design is one Shiny module whose server returns a reactive yielding a `doe_design`. To add one:

1. Write `R/<name>-design.R` implementing the helper contract below. Keep it free of Shiny so every piece is testable on its own. The design must come from an R package — nothing is constructed here.
2. Write `R/<name>-module.R` with `<name>_ui(id)` and `<name>_server(id)`. The UI builds the inputs from the design's own limits and choices; the server returns a reactive yielding the `doe_design`.
3. Add one entry to `design_registry()` in `R/registry.R`.

`R/factorial-design.R` is the reference implementation, and `inst/adding-designs.md` is a step-by-step guide to the whole job — written as instructions to an LLM, but worth reading first either way. It carries the procedure and the traps; the contract below stays the source of truth for the shapes.

### The helper contract

| function | returns | may be empty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{design}_get_packages()` | unnamed `character` of package names | no |
| `{design}_get_limits()` | named `list` of `integer` vectors of length 2, each `c(min, max)` inclusive | no |
| `{design}_get_{option}_choices(...)` | `numeric` of valid values, ascending, optionally named by display label | yes |
| `{design}_get_types(...)` | `character` of ids, best first, named by display label | yes |
| `{design}_create(...)` | a `doe_design` — see `new_design()` | n/a |
| `{design}_get_notes(design)` | unnamed `character`, one note per line | yes |

**The vector holds the values; its names are the labels.** This is the one that bites, because getting it backwards produces a dropdown that looks correct and submits nonsense — Shiny takes names as labels and values as values. Both `_choices()` and `_get_types()` follow it:

```
> factorial_get_num_runs_choices(6)
 8 runs (2^(6-3) fraction) 16 runs (2^(6-2) fraction) 32 runs (2^(6-1) fraction)
                         8                         16                         32

> factorial_get_types(6, 16)
Resolution IV: E=ABC, F=ABD (3 words of length 4)   Resolution III: E=AB, F=ACD ...
                                          "6-2.1"                       "6-2.2"
```

Names are optional on `_choices()`. Supply them only when the value alone does not read well: run counts earn a label, block counts do not, and `factorial_get_blocks_choices()` returns a bare `c(1, 2, 4, 8)`.

Three of the functions can legitimately return nothing, and callers must cope rather than assume at least one element — `_get_types()` especially, since a zero-length result is exactly how `factorial_create()` tells a full factorial from a fraction.

`{design}_get_notes()` takes **the object the package returned**, not a `doe_design`. It runs during construction, since that is where the package's own metadata is still attached.

A `doe_design` from `new_design(table, title, notes)` holds:

- `table` — a `tibble`, one row per run in standard order, carrying none of the package's attributes. `new_design()` coerces whatever you hand it, so a generator need not. Note that coercion does **not** strip other attributes, so still build a clean table rather than passing the package's own object straight through. The order columns are added later by the app, not here.
- `title` — one line, shown above the table.
- `notes` — `character`, zero or more lines shown underneath.

Three of these have shapes that exist because the designs disagree with each other, so do not simplify them away:

**`_get_limits()` returns a named list, not one range.** Only some designs have a single factor-count axis. A crossed array has separate control and noise counts; a mixture design counts components; a Latin square has one size that fixes everything. The factorial returns `list(num_factors = c(2, 127))`, and a crossed array would return `list(control = c(3, 7), noise = c(1, 15))`.

**`_create()` takes named options, with no fixed positional run count.** The number of runs is something the user *chooses* for only a couple of designs — the two-level factorial and the Latin hypercube. For a Box-Behnken, a central composite, a Plackett-Burman or a randomized block it is *derived* from the other options, so those designs must not be made to carry a `num_runs` argument they would have to ignore. Designs that take one accept `num_runs`; the rest do not.

**`_get_types()` may legitimately return nothing.** Of the designs this app is meant to cover, most have no variant to choose between. A full factorial has none either, which is exactly how `factorial_create()` tells a full factorial from a fraction. Callers must handle a zero-length result rather than assuming at least one.

Identify a type by the package's own id, not by position. `factorial_get_types()` returns FrF2 catalog ids like `6-2.1`, so a type left over from a different size is rejected by name. An index would silently select whatever had moved into that slot.

### Naming

Name the two quantities every design shares consistently: `num_runs` for the number of runs and `num_factors` for the number of experimental factors. That applies to function arguments, local variables and Shiny input ids alike, so `input$num_factors` feeds `factorial_create(num_factors = )`. Arguments of the underlying package keep that package's own spelling — `FrF2::FrF2(nruns = , nfactors = )` is called as FrF2 names it, not renamed at the boundary.

Factor names come from two shared helpers in `R/design.R`. `default_factor_names(num_factors)` generates the defaults — single letters while they last, then `names0()`. `rename_factors(text, num_factors)` merges a user's comma-separated names over those defaults. The result feeds `{design}_create()`, which hands it to the package; it must **not** be applied to a finished design instead. FrF2 needs the names at construction for its alias legend to read `A=Temp` rather than `A=A`, and renaming afterwards would leave the notes describing factors by the wrong label.

Each design also names the factor count its panel opens on — `FACTORIAL_DEFAULT_FACTORS`, `SPACEFILLING_OPT_DEFAULT_FACTORS` — because the dependent dropdowns are built from it and the two must not drift apart.

### The packages are the source of truth

Almost all computation happens in the R package implementing the method. This app calls the package, reports what it returns, and formats the result. It does not reimplement, re-derive, or second-guess it — not the designs, not their properties, and not the parameter values they accept.

This is not a style preference. Three things in earlier versions of this code looked perfectly reasonable and were all wrong:

- A definitive screening design built by hand from a Paley conference matrix instead of calling a package.
- The alias structure derived by multiplying every subset of a design's generators — `2^p` words for `p` generators, which hung the app at 53 generators. FrF2 attaches the whole thing to the design under `attr(design, "design.info")$aliased`, bounded by the run count, in 0.11s.
- Available run counts computed as a span of powers of two, when `FrF2::catlg` has irregular gaps — 34 factors has a 2048-run design but no 1024-run one, and asking FrF2 for the missing size errors rather than returning nothing.

Before writing any statistical computation, check whether the package already exposes it. It is easy to miss, because it may arrive as an attribute on an object the package already returned rather than as a function you have to call.

### Limits and error messages

Which parameter values a design accepts is read from its package, not written down in app code. `R/factorial-design.R` derives its factor and run choices from `FrF2::catlg`, so the app follows whichever FrF2 version is installed. This matters because catalogued designs have gaps rather than clean ranges: FrF2 has a 2048-run design for 34 factors but no 1024-run one, and asking it for a size it lacks errors rather than returning nothing.

A *practical* ceiling is fine and belongs with the design that owns it — `FACTORIAL_MAX_RUNS` caps the table at 256 runs, well below the catalog's 4096. Put that sort of limit in the design's own file, never in `R/design.R`.

Three shared helpers in `R/design.R` turn a rejected value into a message worth reading:

- `stop_unavailable(value, available, quantity, context)` — for discrete sets with gaps. Gives `1024 is not an available run count for 34 factors. Choose one of: 64, 128, 256.`
- `stop_out_of_range(value, range, quantity)` — where the valid values really are contiguous and listing them would be noise.
- `stop_unless(condition, message)` — everything else.

Messages are shown to the user in place of the table, so write them for the person running the experiment.

Factor names come from two shared helpers in `R/design.R`. `default_factor_names(num_factors)` generates the defaults — single letters while they last, then `names0()`. `rename_factors(text, num_factors)` merges a user's comma-separated names over those defaults. The result feeds `{design}_create()`, which hands it to the package; it must **not** be applied to a finished design instead. FrF2 needs the names at construction for its alias legend to read `A=Temp` rather than `A=A`, and renaming afterwards would leave the notes describing factors by the wrong label.

Name the two quantities every design shares consistently: `num_runs` for the number of runs and `num_factors` for the number of experimental factors. That applies to function arguments, local variables and Shiny input ids alike, so `input$num_factors` feeds `factorial_design(num_factors = )`. Arguments of the underlying package keep that package's own spelling — `FrF2::FrF2(nruns = , nfactors = )` is called as FrF2 names it, not renamed at the boundary.

Generators return rows in standard order and stay deterministic; `with_run_order()` adds the run-order column afterwards. That separation is what keeps the generator snapshots stable without seeding.

Only the two-level factorial is implemented. Nine further designs — Plackett-Burman, definitive screening, central composite, Box-Behnken, simplex lattice, Latin hypercube, crossed array, randomized block, and Latin square — were removed pending a decision on how to compute them, and are recoverable from git history at `cc3901c`.

---
name: add-doe-design
description: Add a new experimental design, or a new design family, to the doe-ui Shiny app. Use when asked to add a design, wire up a new DOE package, extend the design registry, or add a variant of a design that already exists.
---

# Adding a design to doe-ui

## Read these first

- `README.md`, section "Adding a design" — the helper contract, the return shapes, and the naming rules. That is the source of truth; this file does not repeat it.
- `R/factorial-design.R` — the reference implementation of the contract.

One rule everything below follows from: **the package is the source of truth.** This app calls an R package, reports what it returns, and formats the result. It does not reimplement, re-derive, or second-guess the statistics. If you are about to write a loop that computes a design property, stop and look for it in the package first.

## 1. Is it a new design, or a type within one?

The test: **does switching between them change which inputs are on screen?**

- Different options panel → a separate registry entry. It may join an existing `family` or start a new one.
- Same panel, different argument to the same generator → a `type` within one design, returned by `{design}_get_types()`.

How the current four landed:

| | why |
| --- | --- |
| Latin hypercubes (Optimized) vs (Random) | separate entries — one picks a run count from a list, the other takes any number, so the panels differ |
| Audze-Eglais / Max-Min L1 / Max-Min L2 | types within the optimized entry — same panel, one argument changes |
| Uniform designs | separate entry — not a hypercube, and reaches 15 factors where the hypercube criteria stop at 10 |

Differing *limits* are a strong signal for separate entries. A single entry has to claim the widest range and then fail across the part it cannot serve.

## 2. Establish what the package supports, from the package

Before writing any file, open a console and find out:

**Which combinations exist.** Read the package's own catalog or index — `FrF2::catlg`, `sfd::sfd_lib` — rather than inferring a range from the documentation.

**Whether availability has gaps.** It usually does. FrF2 has a 2048-run design for 34 factors but no 1024-run one, and around half its factor counts have a hole like that. Asking for a missing size errors rather than returning nothing. Never compute the valid values as a span.

**Whether the package already computes the design's properties.** Check attributes on whatever it returns, not only its exported functions. FrF2 attaches the entire alias structure under `attr(design, "design.info")$aliased`; deriving it here instead took `2^p` words for `p` generators and hung the app at 53 generators.

**How long it takes at the largest size you will offer.** Time it. Anything iterative or combinatorial gets timed before it is exposed, not after a user finds it.

**What scale the values come out on.** You will need to declare it, so read it off a built design.

## 3. Write the generator — `R/<name>-design.R`

Pure R, no Shiny, so every piece is testable on its own. Implement the contract from the README. Points that are easy to get wrong:

- `_get_limits()` returns a **named list** of integer pairs. Not every design counts factors — a crossed array has control and noise counts, a mixture design counts components.
- `_get_{option}_choices()` exists only for options whose valid values are constrained. Three of the four current designs have a run-count helper; `spacefilling_rand_*` takes any number in range and has none. Do not invent a helper to list values that are not actually restricted.
- `_get_types()` may return nothing, and empty is meaningful — it is how `factorial_create()` distinguishes a full factorial from a fraction. Callers must cope with zero length.
- Identify a type by **the package's own id**, never by position in a list. An index silently selects whatever moved into that slot when the size changes.
- A practical ceiling of your own is fine. Declare it in the design's own file, label it as ours rather than the package's, and never put it in `R/design.R`.
- Validate with `stop_unless()`, `stop_unavailable()` and `stop_out_of_range()` from `R/design.R`. `stop_unavailable()` lists what *is* available, which is the only honest message when the package has gaps. These messages are shown to the experimenter in place of the table, so write them for that reader.
- Return `new_design(table, title, notes)`. Build the table column by column rather than handing over the package's object: coercion to a tibble does not strip the package's attributes.

## 4. Write the module — `R/<name>-module.R`

`<name>_ui(id)` and `<name>_server(id)`, the server returning a reactive that yields the `doe_design`. Two things bite here:

**Build dependent dropdowns with their choices already in place.** Declare a named default factor count — see `FACTORIAL_DEFAULT_FACTORS` — and compute the dependent choices from it in the UI function. Filling them from an observer alone is not enough: observers fire only when their input *changes*, and reselecting a design rebuilds its UI with the same values, which Shiny's client-side dedup suppresses. The dropdown then arrives empty and stays empty until the user nudges something. Keep the observer too, for when the count really does change.

**Values are the data; names are the labels.** `c("16 runs (2^(6-2) fraction)" = 16)`. Backwards produces a dropdown that displays correctly and submits nonsense.

Guard every reactive on the factor count being usable. `moduleServer()` runs eagerly at startup, so your inputs are `NULL` until the UI is rendered and bound.

## 5. Register it — `R/registry.R`

One entry: `label`, `family`, `ui`, `server`, `packages`. Registry order sets sidebar order, and families appear in the order they are first used. `design_registry()` is a function rather than a list so that source order does not matter — do not turn it back into a list.

## 6. Verify

In this order:

1. `Rscript tests/run.R`.
2. Add the new design to `tests/testthat/test-contract.R` so its return shapes are pinned — that file exists to stop the documented shapes drifting from the code.
3. Snapshot the generator's output and its user-facing error messages. Review the diff; a changed snapshot usually means a changed design.
4. Time the largest size you offer, and assert it in a test if anything about it is iterative.
5. Boot the app and select the design. A broken module panel does **not** show up at startup, because `output$options` renders it lazily — only selecting it will reveal the error.
6. Open the design, switch to another, and switch back. This is what catches empty dropdowns.

## Traps, with the case that produced each

Each of these was a real defect in this repo, not a hypothetical.

**Deriving what the package already knows.** A definitive screening design was built by hand from a Paley conference matrix. The alias structure was derived by multiplying every subset of a design's generators: 16.7 million words at 24 generators, 9e15 at 53, and a frozen app. FrF2 had it attached to the design all along.

**Computing valid values instead of reading them.** Run counts were generated as a span of powers of two. Around half of FrF2's factor counts have a missing size in that span, and asking for one errors.

**Measuring the coded scale instead of declaring it.** A random Latin hypercube in 3 factors and 7 runs spans 0.0131 to 0.9706 — it does not reach its own bounds, and is not supposed to. Any transformation that infers the scale from the observed column range will stretch it to the endpoints and destroy the sampling property.

**Returning indices where you meant values.** A lookup used `which(x != 0)`, which returns positions named by the dimnames — so the run counts ended up as *names* and column positions as *values*. The dropdown looked perfect and submitted nonsense.

**`apply()` over a table that has one row.** It simplifies to a matrix, and lookup by name then fails with `subscript out of bounds`. This happened only at the top of the supported range, where a single design type survived. Use `lapply()`.

**Overloaded package arguments.** `FrF2::FrF2(blocks = )` means "how many blocks" for a double, but a vector of Yates column numbers for an integer, so `blocks = 1L` fails obscurely where `blocks = 1` means unblocked. Coerce deliberately and pin it with a test.

**Labels that are not numbers.** With replications, FrF2 labels blocks `1.1`, `2.1` — block and replicate, not a decimal. Coercing that column to numeric invents data that looks plausible. Leave such columns as character.

## Things that are not designs

The app assumes quantitative factors on a coded scale. A mixture design's components are proportions constrained to sum to one; a randomized block design has treatments, not factors. If you are adding one of those, say so rather than forcing it into the flat-factor model, and check `plans/` for the current thinking on how those should be handled.
